drills.los_text: discuss approaches to setting expectations for fixed-income returns
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 2: Forecasting Asset Class Returns

questions.stem: The three main approaches to forecasting fixed-income returns are most likely:

options.A: Duration matching, immunization, and cash-flow matching.
options.B: Discounted cash flow, risk premium, and equilibrium models.
options.C: Historical averages, forward rates, and consensus surveys.

rationales.A: Duration matching, immunization, and cash-flow matching are liability-driven portfolio management techniques, not methods for forming capital market expectations. They describe how to structure a portfolio once return expectations exist; they say nothing about what returns to expect.
rationales.B: The three approaches are (1) discounted cash flow, which builds the expected return from an asset's cash flows and its price, (2) the risk premium or building block approach, which adds compensation for each risk borne to a baseline short-term default-free rate, and (3) equilibrium models, whose outputs are often useful as the neutral starting point in a Black-Litterman framework.
rationales.C: Historical averages and consensus surveys are inputs to a forecast rather than approaches to building one, and forward-rate methods such as full return decomposition are an implementation of the discounted cash flow approach. The three main approaches are discounted cash flow, the risk premium (building block) approach, and equilibrium models.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager holds a bond portfolio with Macaulay duration of 4.89 years and current YTM of 1%. If yields rise 200 bps immediately and then remain constant, over a horizon equal to the portfolio's Macaulay duration, the realized return will most likely be:

options.A: Well above the initial YTM.
options.B: Well below the initial YTM.
options.C: Close to the initial YTM.

rationales.A: Reinvestment gains do not dominate at a horizon equal to Macaulay duration. They dominate only over horizons longer than Macaulay duration, where reinvestment at the higher rate more than compensates for the initial capital loss.
rationales.B: Capital losses dominate only over horizons shorter than Macaulay duration. The horizon here is 4.89 years, exactly the portfolio's Macaulay duration, so the capital loss from the 200 bp rise in yields is offset rather than dominant.
rationales.C: Macaulay duration is the horizon at which the capital gain or loss effect and the reinvestment effect roughly offset, leaving the realized return close to the original yield to maturity of 1%. The offset is exact when the yield curve is flat and the change in yields is immediate and occurs in a single step; otherwise it is an approximation. Shorter horizons are dominated by the capital loss, longer horizons by reinvestment at the higher rate.

questions.stem: For an investment horizon shorter than a bond's Macaulay duration, a rise in yields most likely leaves the realized return:

options.A: Higher.
options.B: Lower.
options.C: Unchanged.

rationales.A: Rising yields raise the realized return only when the horizon is longer than the bond's Macaulay duration, because reinvestment at the higher rate then outweighs the capital loss. Over a shorter horizon the price decline has not yet been earned back.
rationales.B: Over horizons shorter than Macaulay duration the capital gain or loss effect dominates the reinvestment effect, so rising yields imply a lower realized return and falling yields a higher one.
rationales.C: The two effects offset each other only at a horizon equal to Macaulay duration, and even there the offset is exact only under the assumptions of a flat yield curve and an immediate, single-step change in yields.

questions.stem: The building block approach to fixed-income expected returns identifies four components. These are most likely:

options.A: Short-rate expectation, forward premium, convexity adjustment, and roll yield.
options.B: Risk-free rate, market risk premium, alpha, and expected inflation.
options.C: One-period default-free rate, term premium, credit premium, and liquidity premium.

rationales.A: Short-rate expectations, forward premiums, convexity adjustments, and roll yield are yield-curve decomposition concepts. They describe how a given curve can be taken apart, not the four blocks from which an expected fixed-income return is built.
rationales.B: The market risk premium and alpha belong to an equity return decomposition, and expected inflation is already embedded in the nominal short-term default-free rate rather than added as a separate block.
rationales.C: The four components are the one-period default-free rate, the term premium, the credit premium, and the liquidity premium. The short-term default-free rate is the baseline time-value component; the term premium compensates for bearing duration risk beyond one period; the credit premium compensates for default and downgrade risk; and the liquidity premium compensates for holding an issue that cannot be traded cheaply.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Building Block Approach to Fixed-Income Returns

questions.stem: Which of the four building block components is most likely directly observable in market data?

options.A: The term premium.
options.B: The credit premium.
options.C: The short-term default-free rate.

rationales.A: The term premium is embedded in the slope of the yield curve, but an observed long-minus-short spread also reflects expected changes in short rates, so the premium itself has to be estimated rather than read off the market.
rationales.B: The credit premium is embedded in observed credit spreads, but a spread also compensates for expected default losses and for illiquidity, so the premium is not equal to the observed spread.
rationales.C: Only the short-term default-free rate is potentially observable. It is usually taken to be a government zero-coupon bill at a frequently issued maturity, which trades continuously and is closely tied to the central bank's policy rate. The term, credit, and liquidity premiums are all embedded in prices alongside other compensation and must be estimated.

questions.stem: The indicator with the strongest historical relationship to future excess bond returns at one-quarter, one-year, and five-year horizons is most likely:

options.A: The unemployment rate.
options.B: The yield curve slope.
options.C: The ex ante real yield.

rationales.A: The unemployment rate has the weakest one-year relationship with subsequent excess bond returns, a correlation of about 0.18, the lowest of the eight indicators examined.
rationales.B: The yield curve slope, measured as the 10-year yield minus the 3-month yield, carries some information at short horizons but has essentially no five-year relationship, a correlation of about 0.06.
rationales.C: The ex ante real yield has the strongest relationship with subsequent excess bond returns at every horizon examined: correlations of roughly 0.28 over one quarter, 0.48 over one year, and 0.69 over five years. Its predictive power strengthens as the horizon lengthens, which is what one expects of a valuation measure, since a high real yield is simply a cheap starting point.

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely a driver of the term premium on nominal bonds?

options.A: Momentum in credit spreads.
options.B: Level-dependent inflation uncertainty.
options.C: Ability to hedge recession risk.

rationales.A: Momentum in credit spreads is not one of the drivers of the nominal term premium. The four drivers are level-dependent inflation uncertainty, the ability of bonds to hedge recession risk, bond supply and demand, and cyclical effects.
rationales.B: Level-dependent inflation uncertainty is one of the four drivers: uncertainty about future inflation rises with the level of inflation, and investors demand a larger term premium to bear it.
rationales.C: The ability of bonds to hedge recession risk is one of the four drivers: when bonds pay off in recessions they act as insurance, and the term premium investors require for holding them falls.

questions.stem: When growth and inflation are driven primarily by aggregate supply shocks rather than by aggregate demand shocks, the term premium on nominal bonds is most likely:

options.A: Higher.
options.B: Lower.
options.C: Unaffected.

rationales.A: When growth and inflation are driven primarily by aggregate supply, nominal bond returns tend to be positively correlated with growth: an adverse supply shock pushes inflation up and growth down, so bonds lose value at exactly the moment the economy weakens. Bonds then amplify rather than hedge growth risk, and a higher term premium is necessary to induce investors to hold them.
rationales.B: A lower term premium is warranted in the demand-shock case. There growth and inflation move together, bond returns are negatively correlated with growth, and bonds work as an effective recession hedge.
rationales.C: The source of the shocks is central to the term premium, because it sets the sign of the correlation between bond returns and growth and therefore determines whether bonds hedge or amplify recession risk.

questions.stem: Credit premiums are most likely especially generous at the:

options.A: short end of the credit curve.
options.B: long end of the credit curve.
options.C: intermediate portion of the credit curve.

rationales.A: Credit premiums tend to be especially generous at the short end of the credit curve. Two explanations are offered: event risk, since even an unlikely default would impose a large proportional loss on a short-dated bond whose remaining expected return is small, and the illiquidity of seasoned short-maturity issues. This is the basis of the credit barbell, which takes credit exposure at short maturities and picks up duration risk through long-maturity government bonds.
rationales.B: Greater cumulative default risk over long horizons makes this the intuitive answer, but the historical evidence runs the other way: realized compensation per unit of credit risk has been richest at short maturities, which is precisely why the credit barbell pairs short credit with long government duration.
rationales.C: Compensation for credit risk is not concentrated in the intermediate portion of the curve. It is strongest at the short end, where event risk and the illiquidity of old issues are priced.

questions.stem: Historically, an increase in VIX implied equity volatility is most likely associated with:

options.A: Lower expected excess returns on investment-grade corporate bonds.
options.B: Higher expected excess returns on investment-grade corporate bonds.
options.C: No meaningful change in excess returns on investment-grade corporate bonds.

rationales.A: This reverses the empirical relationship. A spike in implied volatility coincides with depressed prices and elevated risk premiums, and elevated risk premiums are a bullish rather than bearish signal for subsequent excess returns.
rationales.B: Implied equity volatility is positively correlated with subsequent excess returns on US investment-grade corporate bonds, at roughly 0.28 over one quarter and 0.39 over one year. The interpretation is risk-averse pricing: when volatility spikes, investors demand high risk premiums across all markets at once, and those high premiums are the excess returns subsequently earned.
rationales.C: The relationship is meaningful and positive, with correlations of about 0.28 at a one-quarter horizon and 0.39 at a one-year horizon.

drills.los_text: discuss risks faced by investors in emerging market fixed-income securities and the country risk analysis techniques used to evaluate emerging market economies
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 2: Forecasting Asset Class Returns

questions.stem: The two broad categories of risk specific to emerging market debt investments are most likely:

options.A: Market risk and liquidity risk.
options.B: Economic risk and political and legal risk.
options.C: Sovereign risk and corporate risk.

rationales.A: Market risk and liquidity risk attach to bonds everywhere, developed and emerging alike. Neither is specific to emerging market debt, so the pair does not describe the risks that distinguish emerging market borrowers from developed market ones.
rationales.B: Risks specific to emerging market debt sort into two groups. Economic risks speak to the borrower's ability to pay: growth, inflation, fiscal and external balances, the size and currency composition of the debt stock. Political and legal risks speak to the borrower's willingness to pay: sovereign immunity, weak property rights and contract enforcement, confiscation, nationalization, corruption and capital controls. A credit can be sound on the first set and still fail on the second.
rationales.C: Sovereign versus corporate is a split by type of issuer, not by type of risk. Both classes of issuer are exposed to the same ability-to-pay and willingness-to-pay dimensions, so this pair describes who borrows rather than the nature of the risk being analyzed.

questions.stem: A persistent fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio in an emerging market economy most likely becomes a cause for concern when it exceeds:

rationales.A: 2% sits below the guideline. A deficit of this size is routinely run by economies with no fiscal stress at all, so it would flag healthy borrowers and give the analyst no discriminating power.
rationales.B: A fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio persistently above 4% is likely a cause for concern in an emerging market. The word that carries the weight is persistently: a one-off deficit driven by a recession or a specific investment program is not the signal. A deficit held above 4% year after year means the debt stock compounds faster than the economy grows, which eventually forces either higher taxes, spending cuts, inflation or default.
rationales.C: 8% is too high a trigger. By the time deficits of that scale have persisted, the deterioration in debt dynamics is already advanced, and the analyst has lost the warning the indicator is meant to give. The guideline sits at 4%.

questions.stem: A debt-to-GDP ratio most likely becomes a sign of vulnerability for an emerging market economy when it exceeds:

rationales.A: A debt-to-GDP ratio above 70%–80% is a sign of vulnerability for an emerging market, even though a ratio at that level might be only a mild concern for a developed market. The asymmetry is the point: developed sovereigns borrow in their own currency, at longer maturities, from a deep and largely domestic investor base, and can carry far more debt before markets balk. An emerging market with the same ratio is more likely to be funding in hard currency at shorter tenors from investors who can leave quickly.
rationales.B: 40% is below the threshold. Many emerging markets carry debt at this level without strain, so treating it as a vulnerability signal would flag sound borrowers and dilute the indicator.
rationales.C: 150% is well above the threshold. Only a handful of sovereigns, generally developed ones with their own currency and a captive domestic investor base, sustain debt at that level. Setting the trigger there would miss the emerging market distress the guideline is designed to catch. The guideline sits at 70%–80%.

questions.stem: An emerging market's foreign exchange reserves are most likely an ample buffer when reserves as a percentage of short-term debt are at least:

rationales.A: At 50%, reserves cover only half of the debt falling due within a year. The country depends on rolling over the rest, and that rollover is exactly what disappears in a funding stop. This is an inadequate buffer, not an ample one.
rationales.B: Reserves below 100% of short-term debt is the level at which the position becomes risky, so 100% is the floor rather than the comfortable level. Bare coverage leaves nothing for a current account deficit, capital flight or a currency defense occurring at the same time as the maturities.
rationales.C: FX reserves of less than 100% of short-term debt is risky, whereas a ratio greater than 200% is ample. Reserves at twice short-term debt let the authorities meet a full year of maturing hard-currency obligations without market access and still retain a buffer for the current account and for defending the exchange rate, which is what makes the cushion genuinely ample.

questions.stem: A persistent current account deficit for an emerging market becomes a sign of potential lack of competitiveness when it exceeds most likely:

options.A: 10% of GDP.
options.B: 1% of GDP.
options.C: 4% of GDP.

rationales.A: 10% of GDP is far above the guideline. A deficit that large is usually already a crisis in progress rather than an early warning of weakening competitiveness.
rationales.B: 1% of GDP is well below the guideline. Deficits of this size are common in healthy, growing economies importing capital goods, and flagging them would strip the indicator of any discriminating power.
rationales.C: Persistent current account deficits greater than 4% of GDP probably indicate a lack of competitiveness. A deficit must be financed, so a country running one of that size year after year is accumulating external liabilities and depends on continued inflows. If the deficit reflects imports outpacing exports rather than investment that will later generate foreign earnings, the underlying problem is competitiveness, and the usual adjustment is a weaker currency.

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely an economic vulnerability characteristic of emerging market economies?

options.A: Concentrated wealth and income with a narrow tax base.
options.B: Diversified financial markets with sophisticated institutions.
options.C: Reliance on foreign borrowing in hard currencies.

rationales.A: Greater concentration of wealth and income and a less diverse tax base is a listed vulnerability. Revenue that depends on a few taxpayers, sectors or commodities falls sharply in a downturn, precisely when the government most needs it, which makes fiscal outcomes volatile.
rationales.B: Emerging markets are characterized by small and less sophisticated financial markets and institutions, which is the opposite of diversified markets served by a broad set of sophisticated institutions. Shallow markets mean borrowers cannot readily refinance at home, price discovery is poor, and a modest outflow moves prices a long way, so this option describes a strength rather than a vulnerability.
rationales.C: Reliance on foreign borrowing, often in hard currencies that are not the country's own, is a listed vulnerability. Hard-currency debt cannot be inflated away or serviced by printing money, and a depreciation raises the local-currency cost of servicing it at the same time as it tends to weaken the domestic economy.

questions.stem: Political and legal risks that particularly affect emerging market debt investors most likely include:

options.A: Sovereign immunity limiting legal recourse against the borrower.
options.B: IMF membership guaranteeing repayment of sovereign obligations.
options.C: Exchange rate pegs eliminating currency risk for bondholders.

rationales.A: Sovereign immunity makes it very difficult to force a sovereign borrower to pay its debts. There is no bankruptcy court with jurisdiction over a state and few assets a creditor can seize, so recovery depends largely on the sovereign's willingness to pay. Alongside it sit weak property rights, weak contract enforcement, confiscation, nationalization, corruption and capital controls, all of which are political and legal rather than economic in character.
rationales.B: IMF membership carries no guarantee of repayment. Sovereign defaults have occurred among members, and an IMF program typically restructures or reprofiles private claims rather than making them whole. The underlying point is the reverse of this option: legal recourse against a sovereign borrower is limited, not underwritten by an outside institution.
rationales.C: A peg does not eliminate currency risk; it suppresses it until it breaks, and pegs tend to collapse abruptly and by large amounts once reserves run down. Currency regimes are in any case not among the political and legal risks identified, which center on weak enforcement and on willingness to pay.

questions.curriculum_ref: Political and Legal Risks/Willingness to Pay

questions.stem: A foreign debt burden most likely signals danger for an emerging market when it exceeds:

options.A: 100% of GDP or 500% of current account receipts.
options.B: 20% of GDP or 100% of current account receipts.
options.C: 50% of GDP or 200% of current account receipts.

rationales.A: These levels are higher than the guideline. Debt at 100% of GDP or 500% of current account receipts describes a sovereign already in severe external distress, so a trigger set there arrives far too late to be a warning.
rationales.B: These levels are lower than the guideline. Foreign debt of 20% of GDP or one year of current account receipts is carried comfortably by many emerging markets, so flagging it as danger would capture sound borrowers.
rationales.C: Foreign debt greater than 50% of GDP or greater than 200% of current account receipts is a sign of danger. The two tests are complementary: the GDP ratio scales the debt to the size of the economy, while the current account receipts ratio scales it to the hard currency the country actually earns, which is what external debt must ultimately be serviced out of. An economy with a small export base can therefore be stretched by a debt load that looks moderate relative to GDP.

questions.stem: An analyst declines to invest in an emerging market's 10-year local-currency government bond on governance grounds. The circumstance most likely prompting that decision is:

options.A: A record free of nationalization or expropriation.
options.B: A fragile coalition likely to give way to a fiscally undisciplined party.
options.C: A stable single-party government with investor-friendly policies.

rationales.A: A history of never having engaged in nationalization or expropriation reduces political and legal risk rather than raising it. It is evidence for the investment, not a governance reason to decline.
rationales.B: The governance concern has two parts, and both matter over a 10-year horizon. Coalition governments are often unstable, so the current pro-growth policy stance may not survive the term of the bond. The most likely alternative was a return to the previously dominant party, which lacked fiscal discipline and was hostile to investors, and which could undo the pro-growth policies or even disavow the debt. Because the bond is local-currency and long-dated, the investor carries both the risk that fiscal deterioration is monetized through inflation and currency weakness and the risk of outright repudiation.
rationales.C: A stable single-party government pursuing predictable, investor-friendly policies is the opposite of the risk at issue. The concern that drives the decision is coalition instability and the character of the likely successor government.

drills.los_text: discuss approaches to setting expectations for equity investment market returns
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 2: Forecasting Asset Class Returns

questions.stem: Historical equity return statistics used as estimates of expected future returns are most likely:

options.A: Unbiased and efficient.
options.B: Highly reliable.
options.C: Very imprecise.

rationales.A: Historical mean returns are neither unbiased nor efficient estimators of expected future returns across developed and emerging markets. Survivorship and selection effects bias the samples upward, structural change means the return-generating process is not stationary, and the sampling error is large, so the estimates should be treated skeptically rather than taken at face value.
rationales.B: Length of history does not rescue the estimate. Even with more than a century of data the standard error of the mean remains large, because it shrinks only with the square root of the number of observations while the volatility being averaged over stays high. Long histories also span regime changes, so adding years adds as much heterogeneity as information.
rationales.C: Historical mean equity returns across countries range from 5.0% (Austria) to 9.4% (South Africa), yet every one of those values sits inside the 95% confidence interval for every country. Statistically there is no meaningful difference between them: a sample average is a very imprecise estimate of the true mean unless volatility is small relative to that mean, and for equities annual volatility of roughly 15% to 20% against a mean in the high single digits is anything but small. The practical implication is that historical averages cannot by themselves support fine distinctions between markets' expected returns.

questions.curriculum_ref: Historical Statistics Approach to Equity Returns

questions.stem: The components summed in the Grinold–Kroner expected equity return are most likely:

options.A: the risk-free rate, beta times the market risk premium, and alpha.
options.B: dividend yield, per-share earnings growth, and repricing return.
options.C: the capitalization rate and the net operating income growth rate.

rationales.A: This is the capital asset pricing model, E(Re) ≈ rf + β × (Rm − rf) + α. It builds expected return from a risk-free rate, a beta-scaled market premium, and a manager-specific alpha, rather than from the observable cash flow, growth, and valuation components of the equity itself.
rationales.B: The Grinold–Kroner model is E(Re) ≈ D/P + (%ΔE − %ΔS) + %ΔP/E, where D/P is the dividend yield, (%ΔE − %ΔS) is the growth rate of earnings per share, and %ΔP/E is the repricing return from a change in the valuation multiple. Because %ΔS < 0 for net share repurchases, buybacks raise per-share earnings growth above total earnings growth and therefore add to the expected return.
rationales.C: Cap rate plus the growth rate of net operating income is the expected return model for real estate, in which the capitalization rate supplies the income yield. It is not the model applied to public equity.

questions.stem: A rearrangement of the Grinold–Kroner model decomposes the expected equity return into three components that are most likely:

options.A: dividend yield, real growth, and inflation.
options.B: risk-free rate, systematic risk premium, and idiosyncratic residual.
options.C: income return, earnings growth return, and repricing return.

rationales.A: Dividend yield, real growth, and inflation is a different decomposition: it splits the nominal growth term into real and inflation pieces and carries no explicit share-count or repricing component, so it does not reproduce the three Grinold–Kroner terms.
rationales.B: Risk-free rate plus a systematic risk premium plus an idiosyncratic residual is a CAPM-style decomposition of a required return. Grinold–Kroner instead decomposes an expected return into cash flow, earnings growth, and repricing.
rationales.C: The three components are (1) the expected cash flow (income) return = D/P − %ΔS, (2) the expected nominal earnings growth return = %ΔE, and (3) the expected repricing return = %ΔP/E. The sum of the last two constitutes the expected capital gain. In this rearrangement the share-change term sits in the income component, because net repurchases (%ΔS < 0) are a cash return to shareholders alongside dividends.

questions.stem: Cynthia Casey applies the Grinold–Kroner model with these inputs: dividend yield 2.25%, net share repurchase 1%, earnings growth 6%, and P/E multiple expansion 0.25%. The implied expected equity return is closest to:

rationales.A: E(Re) ≈ D/P + (%ΔE − %ΔS) + %ΔP/E = 2.25% + [6.0% − (−1.0%)] + 0.25% = 2.25% + 7.00% + 0.25% = 9.50%. A net repurchase of 1% means %ΔS = −1%, so the share count is shrinking and earnings per share grow 1% faster than total earnings; subtracting a negative %ΔS adds that 1% to the growth term.
rationales.B: This results from treating the 1% net repurchase as net issuance, that is, as %ΔS = +1%, and subtracting it: 2.25% + 6.0% − 1.0% + 0.25% = 7.50%. The sign is reversed; repurchases reduce the share count and raise per-share growth rather than diluting it.
rationales.C: This results from omitting the share-change term entirely: 2.25% + 6.0% + 0.25% = 8.50%. The net repurchase of 1% (%ΔS = −1%) must be included, and it adds 1% to the earnings growth term.

questions.stem: Casey forecasts corporate earnings growth of 6% against nominal GDP growth of 5%, plus P/E expansion of 0.25% a year. These assumptions are most likely:

options.A: plausible over any horizon, including the very long run.
options.B: implausible over any horizon.
options.C: plausible over a decade but not over the very long run.

rationales.A: Earnings cannot grow faster than nominal GDP indefinitely: a persistent 1% growth premium drives the ratio of corporate earnings to GDP up without bound, and a P/E that expands by 0.25% every year rises without bound as well. The assumptions therefore cannot be sustained over the very long run.
rationales.B: Over a finite horizon these inputs are acceptable rather than implausible. Compounded over 10 years, the 1% growth premium lifts the earnings/GDP ratio by only about 10.5%, the share count shrinks about 9.6%, and the P/E rises about 2.5% — all modest and defensible.
rationales.C: Over 10 years the implied drifts are small: the earnings/GDP ratio rises roughly 10.5%, shares outstanding fall roughly 9.6%, and the P/E rises roughly 2.5%, none of which strains credibility. Extended indefinitely, however, the same assumptions imply an ever-rising share of GDP accruing to corporate earnings and an ever-expanding multiple, so they are not plausible for the very long run.

questions.stem: The cyclically adjusted P/E ratio most likely divides the current price level by:

options.A: average inflation-adjusted earnings over the last decade.
options.B: consensus analyst estimates of the coming year's earnings.
options.C: the most recent quarter's earnings.

rationales.A: The cyclically adjusted P/E divides the current price level by the average level of earnings over the previous 10 years, adjusted for inflation, rather than by the most current earnings. Averaging over a full business cycle or more washes out the cyclical swing in earnings and provides a more stable base against which to judge the current market price, which is why CAPE is used to gauge whether a market is expensive or cheap relative to its own history.
rationales.B: Dividing price by consensus estimates of the coming 12 months of earnings gives a forward P/E. That measure depends on analyst forecasts and on where the economy sits in the cycle; CAPE deliberately avoids both by using a 10-year average of realized, inflation-adjusted earnings.
rationales.C: Annualizing the most recent quarter's earnings gives a standard trailing P/E. It is the measure CAPE is designed to replace, because a single quarter is exactly where cyclical distortion in earnings is largest.

questions.stem: The 'equity-versus-bills' premium and the 'equity-versus-bonds' premium most likely differ by:

options.A: the credit premium in corporate bond yields.
options.B: the term premium in default-free bond returns.
options.C: the country risk premium for the market in question.

rationales.A: A credit premium compensates for default and downgrade risk on corporate bonds. Neither definition of the equity premium is built on corporate credit, so the credit premium is not what separates them.
rationales.B: The two definitions differ by the term premium built into the expected return on default-free bonds. Measuring equity against bonds is an incremental, building-block approach: the bond return already contains the term premium, so the equity premium measured against it is the extra compensation for equity risk alone. Measuring equity against bills instead produces a single composite premium that bundles the term premium together with the compensation for equity risk.
rationales.C: A country risk premium compensates for political, legal, and macroeconomic risk in a particular market and would apply to both definitions alike, so it cannot be the source of the differential between them.

questions.stem: The Singer–Terhaar model of expected equity returns is best described as:

options.A: a factor model using size, value, and momentum risk factors.
options.B: a weighted blend of integrated and segmented CAPM premiums.
options.C: a purely domestic CAPM.

rationales.A: Size, value, and momentum belong to the multifactor family of return models. Singer–Terhaar is built on the CAPM and on the degree of market integration, not on style factors.
rationales.B: Singer–Terhaar combines two underlying CAPMs: one assuming full global integration, in which every asset is priced against a single global market portfolio, and one assuming complete segmentation, in which the asset is priced in isolation against its own local market. The final risk premium is the weighted average RP_i = φ × RP_i^G + (1 − φ) × RP_i^S, where φ is the degree of integration. Segmented pricing gives the larger premium, because the investor cannot diversify away the asset's own volatility, so a lower φ raises the expected return.
rationales.C: A purely domestic CAPM prices an asset against its home market alone. That is only the fully segmented half of Singer–Terhaar; the model also carries an integrated global component and weights the two by φ.

questions.curriculum_ref: Risk Premium Approaches to Equity Returns

questions.stem: Developed-market equities are most likely assigned a Singer–Terhaar integration parameter (φ) in the range:

rationales.A: A φ in the region of 0.50–0.75 reflects partial integration and is the range customarily suggested for emerging market equities and bonds, which are less fully integrated into global markets than developed markets are.
rationales.B: Developed market equities and bonds are highly, though not perfectly, integrated into global markets, so a φ of about 0.75–0.90 is reasonable. The remaining 0.10–0.25 weight on the segmented premium keeps a modest allowance for local pricing, since no market is perfectly integrated.
rationales.C: A φ of 0.10–0.30 describes a market that is largely segmented and priced locally. Applying it to developed markets would put most of the weight on the segmented CAPM and overstate the equity risk premium.

questions.curriculum_ref: Risk Premium Approaches to Equity Returns

questions.stem: For German equities with volatility of 17%, correlation with the global market of 0.70, an integration parameter of 0.85, a global Sharpe ratio of 0.30, and a segmented-market Sharpe ratio of 0.35, the Singer–Terhaar blended equity risk premium is closest to:

rationales.A: This is the fully segmented component on its own: RP_i^S = σ_i × Sharpe_S = 17.0% × 0.35 = 5.95%. Under complete segmentation the correlation with the global market drops out, because none of the asset's volatility can be diversified away globally, which is why this figure is the largest of the three. It must still be weighted by (1 − φ) = 0.15.
rationales.B: This is the fully integrated component on its own: RP_i^G = ρ_(i,GM) × σ_i × Sharpe_G = 0.70 × 17.0% × 0.30 = 3.57%. Only the portion of volatility correlated with the global market is compensated here. It must still be weighted by φ = 0.85 and combined with the segmented premium.
rationales.C: Fully integrated: RP_i^G = 0.70 × 17.0% × 0.30 = 3.57%. Fully segmented: RP_i^S = 17.0% × 0.35 = 5.95%. Blending with φ = 0.85 gives RP_i = (0.85 × 3.57%) + (0.15 × 5.95%) = 3.03% + 0.89% = 3.93%. Because Germany is treated as highly integrated, the result sits close to the integrated premium and only slightly above it.

questions.curriculum_ref: Risk Premium Approaches to Equity Returns

drills.los_text: discuss risks faced by investors in emerging market equity securities
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 2: Forecasting Asset Class Returns

questions.stem: In global equity markets, the relative importance of country effects and global industry effects is most likely:

options.A: approximately equal in all markets.
options.B: weighted toward country effects, especially in emerging markets.
options.C: weighted toward industry effects in developed and emerging markets alike.

rationales.A: The evidence points to an asymmetry rather than a balance: country effects are, on the whole, the stronger of the two, and the gap widens in emerging markets. Treating the two as equal everywhere ignores that pattern.
rationales.B: The empirical evidence here is vast and contradictory, but on the whole country effects still tend to be more important than global industry effects. The asymmetry is sharpest for emerging markets, which are less fully integrated into the global economy and global capital markets, so local policy, currency, and macroeconomic conditions drive returns more than an issuer's industry does.
rationales.C: Industry effects have grown in importance with global integration and matter most where integration is furthest advanced, but they do not dominate country effects generally, and least of all in emerging markets, where country effects are strongest.

questions.stem: For emerging market equity investors, the most consequential political, legal, and regulatory weakness is most likely:

options.A: sovereign immunity barring enforcement of collateral claims.
options.B: weak corporate governance permitting misuse of company assets.
options.C: mandatory dual-listing rules that fragment trading liquidity.

rationales.A: Sovereign immunity limits creditors' recourse when a sovereign borrower does not pay, so it is a weakness emphasized for emerging market debt investors rather than for equity investors. Equity holders are not creditors with collateral claims to enforce; their exposure to the legal environment runs through the protection of minority ownership rights, not through debt remedies.
rationales.B: Weak corporate governance standards are the political, legal, and regulatory weakness that bears most directly on emerging market equity investors, because they allow interested parties to manipulate company capital structures and to misuse business assets. Minority shareholders have no claim on specific cash flows, so when controlling parties can divert value through related-party transactions, dilutive issuance, or asset transfers, the residual claim the equity investor holds can be eroded without any default occurring. The companion weaknesses are disclosure practices that favor insiders and accounting standards that fall short of international norms.
rationales.C: Dual-listing mandates are not among the identified emerging market weaknesses, and fragmented liquidity across exchanges is a market-structure issue rather than a political, legal, or regulatory failing. The weaknesses that matter for equity investors are weak corporate governance, disclosure practices that favor insiders, and inadequate accounting standards.

questions.stem: Relative to emerging market debt investors, the risks on which emerging market equity investors must focus are best described as:

options.A: identical to those facing debt investors.
options.B: limited to currency risk once country credit risk is assessed.
options.C: broader than credit and counterparty risk, especially in times of distress.

rationales.A: The two risk sets overlap but are not identical, so a country credit analysis built for debt does not suffice for equity. Debt analysis is organized around a defined obligation and the borrower's ability and willingness to meet it; equity has no defined obligation, so the analysis must extend to how the residual claim is treated by controlling shareholders, courts, and governments.
rationales.B: Currency risk is one exposure among several, not the whole of the incremental equity risk. Weak corporate governance, thin or insider-favoring disclosure, inadequate accounting standards, weak property rights, and unpredictable regulatory action all affect equity values, and they bite hardest precisely in periods of macroeconomic and political distress, when currency moves are only one of several simultaneous shocks.
rationales.C: Emerging market debt investors focus on the ability and the willingness of the borrower to pay specific obligations. Emerging market equity investors have to focus on a variety of risks beyond traditional credit and counterparty risks, and this is especially true in times of macroeconomic and political distress, when governments and controlling shareholders face strong incentives to protect themselves at the expense of outside equity holders. That is why the equity analysis adds governance, transparency, property rights, and policy-stability considerations to the credit work.

questions.stem: An emerging market's rapid growth is most likely to prove unsustainable when that growth is driven primarily by:

options.A: broad productivity improvements across all sectors.
options.B: conservative monetary policy and a strong fiscal position.
options.C: a widening fiscal deficit and foreign-capital-financed investment spending.

rationales.A: Productivity-driven growth is the sustainable case and the opposite of the structural weakness at issue. Growth that comes from rising output per unit of input does not depend on continued deficit spending or on continued willingness of foreign investors to fund domestic investment, so it does not carry the reversal risk the question is about.
rationales.B: Conservative monetary policy and a sound fiscal position support sustainability rather than undermining it. The economy that illustrates this risk has the opposite profile: poor fiscal discipline, with government spending growing faster than the revenue base can support.
rationales.C: Rapid growth driven by a large and growing fiscal deficit, particularly by rapidly rising redistributive social payments, and by investment spending financed with foreign capital, is vulnerable from both ends. When the government is eventually forced to tighten fiscal policy, the demand that redistributive payments were supporting disappears; and when foreign capital flows shrink, the investment spending they were funding stops. Either reversal hits the domestic economy hard, so the headline growth rate overstates the economy's underlying capacity and the equity investor is underestimating the structural risk embedded in it.

questions.stem: For an emerging market equity investor, the accounting standard-setting arrangement that most likely signals a transparency risk is one composed of:

options.A: the heads of the three largest domestic accounting firms.
options.B: an independent international body of certified public accountants.
options.C: government-appointed regulators separate from the audit profession.

rationales.A: When local accounting standards are set by the auditing firms themselves, and specifically by the heads of the three largest domestic firms, the standard-setter and the audited profession are the same group. That self-regulation creates a direct conflict of interest: the firms whose audit work would be constrained by demanding standards are the firms writing the standards. A requirement that listed companies publish two years of statements conforming to such standards therefore offers much weaker assurance than it appears to, and it is a transparency and governance risk for an outside equity investor who must rely on reported figures.
rationales.B: An independent international body of certified public accountants is the arrangement that reduces rather than signals transparency risk, because the standard-setter is separate from the firms being regulated and the standards are comparable across markets. It is not the arrangement at issue in a market whose standards are set by its own audit firms.
rationales.C: Government-appointed regulators kept separate from the audit profession also break the self-regulatory conflict, since those who write the standards do not earn audit fees under them. The transparency risk arises from self-regulation by the audit firms, not from government oversight.

questions.stem: Because emerging markets are generally less fully integrated into the global economy, their equity risk and return are most likely:

options.A: perfectly correlated with developed market risk and return.
options.B: dominated by global factors, making country selection irrelevant.
options.C: influenced more by local factors than in developed markets.

rationales.A: Emerging market correlations with developed markets are significant but far from perfect, and perfect correlation would leave no diversification benefit and no scope for country-specific outcomes, which is contrary to observed behavior.
rationales.B: This reverses the implication of incomplete integration. If global factors dominated, country selection would add little; because integration is incomplete, country-specific conditions matter more, not less.
rationales.C: Because emerging markets are generally less fully integrated into the global economy, local economic and market factors exert greater influence on risk and return in these markets than they do in developed markets. The practical consequences follow from that: country analysis carries more weight, country-level diversification is more valuable, and a global factor model calibrated on developed markets will explain less of the variation in emerging market returns.

questions.stem: Weak checks and balances on government actions in emerging markets most likely create a risk of:

options.A: property seizure, nationalization, and unpredictable regulation.
options.B: excessive regulation and onerous disclosure requirements.
options.C: large buybacks and shareholder-friendly capital returns.

rationales.A: Weak property rights laws, the lack of enforcement of the laws that exist, and weak checks and balances on governmental action together make seizure of property, nationalization of companies, and prejudicial and unpredictable regulatory action possible. These are the political, legal, and regulatory exposures that can destroy equity value without any deterioration in the operating business, which is why they are assessed separately from the fundamental analysis.
rationales.B: The risk runs in the opposite direction: regulation in these markets is typically weak, inconsistently applied, and unpredictable, rather than excessive or demanding in its disclosure requirements. Thin disclosure that favors insiders is one of the identified weaknesses, so excessive disclosure is the reverse of the problem.
rationales.C: Returning capital to shareholders is not a risk created by weak checks and balances on government action. Where governance and legal protections are weak, the concern is the opposite, that value is diverted away from minority shareholders rather than distributed to them.

questions.stem: A small emerging equity market's listed universe is weighted toward commodity producers, and most of its listed firms floated only minority stakes. Its concentration risk most likely arises from:

options.A: sector dominance combined with a limited free float.
options.B: a single global technology company dominating the market.
options.C: a market of small-cap firms with no large-cap exposure.

rationales.A: In the market at issue roughly half of the public equity market capitalization is represented by companies in the natural resources sector, and the other half is a mix of firms that remain closely held after floating only minority stakes. That produces two concentrations at once. The sector concentration means the whole market is largely a leveraged bet on commodity prices, so diversifying across names within the market does little to diversify the underlying risk. The ownership concentration adds corporate governance and expropriation risk, because dominant shareholders retain control and the minority stake an outside investor buys depends on their restraint.
rationales.B: A single global technology company is not the concentration described in this market, whose listed universe is weighted toward natural resource producers and closely held firms rather than toward one large technology issuer.
rationales.C: An absence of large-cap firms is not the concentration described either. The market contains substantial large companies, including the natural resource producers; the problem is how narrowly the market capitalization is distributed across sectors and how tightly control is held, not a missing size segment.

drills.los_text: explain how economic and competitive factors can affect expectations for real estate investment markets and sector returns
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 2: Forecasting Asset Class Returns

questions.stem: Because properties trade infrequently and appraisals reflect slowly moving averages of past conditions, observed real estate returns most likely result in:

options.A: upward-biased volatility estimates and overstated correlations.
options.B: downward-biased volatility estimates and understated correlations.
options.C: unbiased volatility estimates and unbiased correlation estimates.

rationales.A: The bias runs in the opposite direction. Smoothing suppresses the period-to-period variation in the series, so it cannot raise measured volatility, and it delays rather than sharpens the response to market information, so it cannot raise measured contemporaneous correlation.
rationales.B: Appraisal-based smoothing does not generally bias the mean return, but it significantly distorts estimates of volatility and of correlations. Because each appraisal is a slowly moving average of past conditions, successive observations move far less than true values do and the sample volatility substantially understates the true volatility. The smoothing also disguises the timing of the response to market information, spreading a single shock across several reporting periods, so the strength of contemporaneous correlations with other market variables is understated as well. Used without adjustment, such a series makes real estate look both safer and more diversifying than it is, and an optimizer fed these inputs will over-allocate to it.
rationales.C: The estimates are not unbiased. The mean return is largely unaffected, but volatility and correlation estimates are both distorted downward by the smoothing.

questions.stem: The capitalization rate on a real estate property is best described as:

options.A: annual gross rental income divided by the acquisition price.
options.B: current-period net operating income divided by the property value.
options.C: net operating income plus expected growth, divided by the property price.

rationales.A: Gross rental income is not net operating income, since it is measured before the operating expenses that net operating income deducts. The denominator is wrong as well: the cap rate uses the current property value, not the price paid at acquisition, so a cap rate computed on historical cost would drift away from the market measure as values changed.
rationales.B: The cap rate is net operating income in the current period divided by the property value. It is the real estate analogue of EBITDA divided by enterprise value for a corporate issuer, which is why it is used as a valuation yardstick across properties. It is not strictly a cash flow yield, because a portion of net operating income may be reinvested in the property rather than distributed to the owner.
rationales.C: Adding an expected growth term to the numerator confuses the cap rate with the expected return it feeds into. The cap rate itself is a current-income yield; growth enters later, when the cap rate is combined with expected net operating income growth to give a long-run expected return.

questions.stem: With net operating income growing at a constant rate, the long-run expected return on real estate is best described as:

options.A: the cap rate minus the net operating income growth rate.
options.B: the cap rate multiplied by one plus the net operating income growth rate.
options.C: the cap rate plus the net operating income growth rate.

rationales.A: Subtracting growth is the wrong sign. Growth in net operating income raises the total return an owner earns on top of the current income yield, so it adds to the cap rate rather than reducing it. Subtraction would imply that a property with faster-growing income offers a lower expected return.
rationales.B: This is not the algebraic form the Gordon growth model produces. The model adds the growth rate to the income yield; it does not scale the yield by one plus growth, which would make the growth contribution proportional to the cap rate rather than additive to it.
rationales.C: Applying the Gordon growth model to real estate under a constant net operating income growth assumption gives the expected return as the cap rate plus the net operating income growth rate, the same structure as the dividend yield plus growth formulation used for equities. The cap rate supplies the current income yield and the growth term supplies the expected appreciation that comes with rising net operating income. In calibrating the growth input, the long-run steady-state growth rate of net operating income should be reasonably close to the nominal growth rate of GDP, since rents cannot outpace the economy indefinitely.

questions.stem: The classic boom–bust cycle in real estate most likely arises from:

options.A: Short construction lead times that absorb excess supply within months.
options.B: Perfectly flexible leases that let rents adjust instantly to demand.
options.C: Overbuilding followed by slow absorption of excess supply.

rationales.A: Construction lead times in real estate are long rather than short, and excess supply is absorbed slowly rather than within months. Property has a very long physical life, so unneeded space does not disappear; it is immobile, so supply cannot be moved to where demand is; and leases are typically multi-year and staggered across tenants, so space returns to the market only gradually. Those features are precisely what prolongs the bust phase.
rationales.B: Leases are not flexible. They are typically written for multiple years and are staggered across tenants, so contractual rents roll over only gradually and cannot adjust instantly when demand falls. That slow adjustment is part of the reason excess supply persists once it has been built.
rationales.C: The cycle runs as follows: perceptions of rising demand and profitability induce new property development, which itself helps sustain the economy; optimism carries that development into overbuilding; property values, lease rates, and occupancy then decline; and the resulting excess supply is absorbed only slowly, because property has a very long life and is immobile and because leases are typically for multiple years and staggered across tenants.

questions.stem: Real estate is a very long-lived asset with high effective duration, so it must earn a term premium. It most likely must also earn:

options.A: A credit premium, an equity risk premium, and a liquidity premium.
options.B: An equity risk premium only.
options.C: No premium beyond the term premium.

rationales.A: Real estate must earn a significant term premium because it is very long-lived with high effective duration. It must also earn a credit premium, because an income-earning property exposes the owner to tenant credit risk — the landlord demands what the average tenant would have to pay to issue such debt; a significant equity risk premium, because the owner bears the full fluctuation in property value along with lease and vacancy uncertainty; and a liquidity premium, because direct property trades infrequently and at high transaction cost.
rationales.B: An equity risk premium is indeed required, but it is not the only premium beyond the term premium. Tenant credit risk calls for a credit premium, and the infrequency and cost of direct property transactions call for a liquidity premium as well.
rationales.C: The term premium is not the only premium required. Beyond compensation for duration, direct real estate also requires a credit premium for tenant credit risk, a significant equity risk premium for property-value, lease, and vacancy uncertainty, and a liquidity premium for the infrequency and cost of transacting.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Risk Premium Perspective on Real Estate Expected Return

questions.stem: For direct real estate with liquidity available on average every two years, a reasonable liquidity premium is closest to:

rationales.A: 0.60% is the estimate that corresponds to quarterly average liquidity, the most liquid case in the estimates cited. Liquidity available only every two years warrants substantially more compensation than that.
rationales.B: 6% is the estimate that corresponds to liquidity available on average only every ten years, a far less liquid case than a two-year horizon.
rationales.C: Ang, Papanikolaou, and Westerfield (2014) suggest liquidity premiums of 0.60% for quarterly liquidity and 0.90% for annual liquidity, rising to 2%, 4%, and 6% for liquidity available on average every 2, 5, and 10 years, respectively. A two-year horizon therefore maps to roughly 2%, and a liquidity premium in the 2%–4% range would seem reasonable for commercial real estate overall.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Risk Premium Perspective on Real Estate Expected Return

questions.stem: Cap rates on direct real estate are most likely:

options.A: Purely countercyclical, always rising during business expansions.
options.B: Pro-cyclical, but mitigated by countercyclical credit spreads.
options.C: Insensitive to interest rates and credit conditions.

rationales.A: Cap rates are pro-cyclical, not countercyclical. They reflect long-term discount rates and therefore tend to rise and fall with the general level of long-term interest rates, which typically rise in expansions rather than fall. It is credit spreads, not cap rates, that behave countercyclically.
rationales.B: Cap rates reflect long-term discount rates, so they should rise and fall with the general level of long-term interest rates, which makes them pro-cyclical. They are also sensitive to credit spreads and to the availability of credit, and because credit spreads are countercyclical — widening in downturns, narrowing in expansions — that sensitivity mitigates the cyclicality of cap rates. Higher vacancy rates also induce higher cap rates.
rationales.C: Cap rates respond to both. They move with the general level of long-term interest rates, because they reflect long-term discount rates, and they are separately sensitive to credit spreads and to the availability of credit.

questions.stem: Incorporating real estate into an equilibrium framework such as the Singer–Terhaar model most likely requires:

options.A: Desmoothing the risk and return data and adding a liquidity premium.
options.B: Treating real estate as a purely global rather than a local asset.
options.C: Using appraisal-based volatility and correlations as reported.

rationales.A: Three considerations apply. First, the impact of smoothing must be removed from real estate risk and return data, because appraisal-based series understate volatility and including them unadjusted distorts the results for every asset class in the exercise, not just real estate. Second, equilibrium models implicitly assume perfectly liquid assets, so adjusting the equilibrium for illiquidity by adding a liquidity premium is important. Third, real estate is location-specific and may be more closely related to local factors than to global ones.
rationales.B: This points in the wrong direction: real estate is location-specific and may be more closely related to local than to global factors, so treating it as purely global misstates its risk. The adjustments actually required are removing the smoothing from the data and adding a liquidity premium.
rationales.C: Appraisal-based volatilities and correlations are smoothed and understate true risk, so using them as reported distorts the equilibrium results for all asset classes. The smoothing must be removed before the data enter the model.

questions.stem: The unusual character of the US commercial real estate crash that followed the global financial crisis is most likely attributable to:

options.A: Capital markets forces, excess leverage, and speculative property investment.
options.B: Unusually restrictive lending standards that limited overbuilding.
options.C: A typical boom–bust cycle in real estate fundamentals.

rationales.A: Clayton et al. (2011) suggested that this crash was the first to be driven by the capital markets rather than by a boom–bust in real estate fundamentals. The catalyst was excess leverage together with investment in more speculative property types. Both the collapse and the recovery were unusually rapid, which is attributed to appraisers responding more vigorously than before to signals from the REIT and commercial mortgage-backed securities markets.
rationales.B: Lending standards were not restrictive. Excess leverage, not a shortage of it, was the catalyst, alongside investment in more speculative property types, and the crash was driven by capital markets forces rather than by restrained overbuilding.
rationales.C: This describes the traditional pattern that the crash departed from. It was the first such episode driven by the capital markets rather than by a boom–bust in real estate fundamentals, and both its collapse and its recovery were unusually rapid.

questions.stem: When compared with unlevered direct real estate, REITs are most likely to offer:

options.A: Lagging returns with significantly lower volatility.
options.B: Weaker performance in exchange for greater liquidity.
options.C: Similar or higher returns with far superior liquidity.

rationales.A: This does not match the evidence. Unlevered REIT returns do not lag the direct market, and REIT volatility is higher rather than lower: direct property returns are appraisal based and smoothed, which understates their measured volatility, whereas REIT prices are marked continuously in public markets.
rationales.B: REIT investors are not sacrificing performance to obtain the liquidity that REITs afford. Aggregate mean returns are comparable across the two forms of ownership — about 8.80% for direct real estate against 9.29% for unlevered REITs — so the liquidity comes without a return penalty.
rationales.C: Aggregate mean returns are comparable, about 8.80% for direct real estate against 9.29% for unlevered REITs, which supports the point that REIT investors are not sacrificing performance to obtain the liquidity afforded by REITs. They obtain similar or slightly higher aggregate returns together with liquidity far superior to that of direct ownership.

drills.los_text: discuss major approaches to forecasting exchange rates
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 2: Forecasting Asset Class Returns

questions.stem: The influence of trade flows, exports minus imports, on contemporaneous exchange rate movements is most likely:

options.A: Significant, because trade flows dominate foreign exchange transactions.
options.B: Strong but lagged, because trade invoices settle at quarter-end.
options.C: Modest, because trade flows are small relative to financial flows.

rationales.A: This overstates the influence of trade flows. They do not dominate foreign exchange transactions: net trade flows are typically small relative to the size of the economy and small relative to actual and potential financial flows, so their contemporaneous influence on exchange rates is modest.
rationales.B: Settlement timing is not the mechanism. The point is one of scale, not of lag: net trade flows are small relative to actual and potential financial flows, so their contemporaneous influence is modest rather than strong but delayed.
rationales.C: Trade flows do not, in general, exert a significant impact on contemporaneous exchange rate movements, provided they can be financed. Net trade flows are typically much smaller than the economy and much smaller than the actual and potential financial flows available to offset them. If trade-related flows do become large relative to financing and investment flows, that usually indicates an emerging crisis rather than normal conditions.

questions.curriculum_ref: Focus on Goods and Services, Trade, and the Current Account

questions.stem: Purchasing power parity (PPP), as applied to exchange rates, is most likely the proposition that:

options.A: The expected change in the exchange rate equals the nominal interest rate differential.
options.B: The expected change in the exchange rate equals the expected inflation differential.
options.C: The nominal exchange rate always equals the ratio of the two money supplies.

rationales.A: Equality between the expected change in the exchange rate and the difference in nominal interest rates is the interest rate parity, or uncovered interest rate parity, relationship. PPP is stated in terms of inflation differentials, not interest rate differentials.
rationales.B: Relative PPP states that the expected percentage change in the exchange rate should equal the difference in expected inflation rates. Equivalently, because the real exchange rate is the ratio of price levels converted into a common currency, PPP says that the expected change in the real exchange rate should be zero.
rationales.C: PPP relates exchange rates to relative price levels, and hence to expected inflation differentials, rather than to the ratio of the two countries' money supplies. It also holds at best as a long-run tendency, not as a relationship that binds at every point in time.

questions.stem: Empirically, PPP is most likely a:

options.A: Consistently accurate predictor at all horizons.
options.B: Poor short-horizon predictor but a better multi-year guide.
options.C: Reliable predictor over daily and weekly horizons.

rationales.A: PPP is not consistently accurate. It is a poor predictor over short to intermediate horizons, and it becomes a useful guide only as the horizon lengthens to several years.
rationales.B: PPP is a poor predictor of exchange rates over short to intermediate horizons but a better guide to currency movements over progressively longer multi-year horizons. Its influence tends to be most evident when inflation differentials are large, persistent, and driven primarily by monetary conditions.
rationales.C: Over daily and weekly horizons PPP has essentially no predictive power; it is a poor short-run predictor and becomes a better guide only over progressively longer multi-year horizons.

questions.stem: Uncovered interest rate parity (UIP) asserts that the expected percentage change in the exchange rate equals the nominal interest rate differential. The empirical evidence on UIP most likely indicates that:

options.A: UIP predicts exchange rate changes well.
options.B: Carry trades earn profits, contradicting UIP.
options.C: Carry trades lose money, confirming UIP.

rationales.A: UIP does not hold up empirically. If it did, the nominal interest rate differential would be an unbiased predictor of the subsequent exchange rate change, and a position that borrowed in the low-rate currency and lent in the high-rate currency would earn nothing on average. Neither result holds in the data.
rationales.B: Empirical evidence consistently shows that carry trades, which borrow in low-rate currencies and lend in high-rate currencies, earn meaningful profits on average, contradicting UIP. Burnside et al. (2011) documented carry-trade returns of 4.31% per year against the USD and 2.88% per year against the GBP over 1976 to 2009. The profitability is usually ascribed to a risk premium, which is consistent with the idea that risk premiums matter for exchange rates.
rationales.C: The evidence runs the other way. Carry trades have been profitable on average rather than loss-making, so the historical record contradicts UIP rather than confirming it.

questions.stem: Hot money flows—vigorous capital flows in response to interest rate differentials—are most likely problematic for central banks because:

options.A: they simplify monetary policy transmission.
options.B: they reduce exchange rate volatility.
options.C: they limit monetary policy effectiveness.

rationales.A: Hot money complicates policy rather than simplifying it. Under the Mundell-Fleming model with free capital flows, a central bank cannot set its policy rate independently of world rates without the exchange rate absorbing the difference, so the flows cost it monetary independence and also draw in short-term speculative capital.
rationales.B: The flows increase exchange rate volatility rather than reduce it. Rapid inflows and their equally rapid reversals whipsaw the currency, and overshooting is nearly inevitable.
rationales.C: Three problems follow from hot money flows: (1) they limit the effectiveness of monetary policy, because under Mundell-Fleming with free capital flow the central bank cannot pursue an independent interest rate policy; (2) the availability of cheap short-term financing may encourage firms to fund long-term needs with short-term money, setting the stage for a crisis when that financing dries up; and (3) the nearly inevitable currency overshooting disrupts non-financial businesses.

questions.stem: When hot money flows into a country and the central bank wishes to prevent excessive currency appreciation and inflation, it will most likely:

options.A: raise policy rates aggressively.
options.B: buy foreign currency and sell government securities.
options.C: sell foreign currency and buy government securities.

rationales.A: Raising policy rates would widen the interest rate differential and attract still more inflows, worsening the very pressure the central bank is trying to contain.
rationales.B: When hot money flows in, central banks may intervene by buying foreign currency, which offsets the upward pressure on the exchange rate, and selling government securities to sterilize the effect on domestic liquidity, thereby limiting the growth of bank reserves or maintaining a target level of interest rates. When hot money flows out, the operations reverse: the central bank sells foreign currency and buys government securities.
rationales.C: This pair of operations is the response to hot money flowing out, not in. Selling foreign currency supports a currency under downward pressure, and buying securities restores the domestic liquidity that outflows have drained.

questions.stem: The 'portfolio balance' perspective on exchange rates argues that in the long run, the relative size of each currency portfolio in the global market depends most likely on:

options.A: fixed exchange rate targets set by international agreement.
options.B: central bank reserves alone.
options.C: relative trend growth rates and current account balances.

rationales.A: Fixed exchange rate agreements are a policy regime, not a determinant of the long-run portfolio balance. The portfolio balance perspective is about the stock of assets investors are willing to hold in each currency, which an agreed target does not set.
rationales.B: Official reserves are one source of demand for a currency's assets, but they are small relative to private holdings and are not the primary long-run driver of each currency portfolio's relative size.
rationales.C: In the long run the relative size of each currency portfolio depends primarily on relative trend growth rates and current account balances. Rapid economic growth expands the share of the global market portfolio denominated in that currency, and large persistent current account deficits also gradually shift currency shares, since the deficit country issues claims that the rest of the world must absorb.

questions.curriculum_ref: Portfolio Balance, Portfolio Composition, and Sustainability Issues

questions.stem: Reserve currency status, such as that held by the US dollar, most likely:

options.A: requires the reserve-currency country to run no current account deficit.
options.B: allows a small current account deficit to supply global liquidity.
options.C: guarantees permanent appreciation of the reserve currency.

rationales.A: Reserve-currency status accommodates a modest current account deficit rather than requiring that the deficit be zero. A persistent small deficit is in fact one way the reserve asset reaches the rest of the world.
rationales.B: A few currencies, notably the USD, have a special status because most official reserves are held in them, the associated sovereign debt is viewed as a safe haven, major commodities are priced in them, and international trade often settles in them. A small current account deficit in a reserve-currency country is welcome, since it helps provide liquidity to the global financial system. Historically, however, reserve currency status has not proven to be permanent.
rationales.C: Reserve status supports demand for the currency's assets but guarantees nothing about its path. Reserve currencies have depreciated over long stretches, and the status itself has shifted from one currency to another over history.

questions.curriculum_ref: Portfolio Balance, Portfolio Composition, and Sustainability Issues

questions.stem: When investors perceive that a currency's underlying assets offer higher risk-adjusted returns, the initial surge of capital most likely:

options.A: drives the exchange rate down immediately.
options.B: leaves the exchange rate unchanged.
options.C: drives the exchange rate up past its equilibrium level.

rationales.A: The direction is the opposite. Capital moving toward the currency's assets must be converted into that currency, which bids it up rather than down.
rationales.B: Capital flows have a strong effect on the exchange rate. A surge of inflows cannot be absorbed without moving the price of the currency.
rationales.C: When a currency's assets are perceived as offering higher risk-adjusted returns, the initial surge of capital drives the exchange rate higher, often to a level from which it is more likely to depreciate than to continue appreciating. This is the overshooting pattern: the currency appreciates far enough that the expectation of subsequent depreciation is what equalizes risk-adjusted expected returns across currencies.

questions.stem: The monetary approach to exchange rates most likely rests on two assumptions:

options.A: UIP holds, and interest rates equal the global risk-free rate.
options.B: Exchange rates are fixed, and capital controls are maintained.
options.C: PPP holds, and inflation is determined by the money supply.

rationales.A: Uncovered interest rate parity is not one of the monetary approach's assumptions, and nothing in that approach requires interest rates to equal a single global risk-free rate. UIP is a separate relationship, and empirically a poor one.
rationales.B: Fixed exchange rates and capital controls are two of the three legs of the impossible trinity, which concerns the policy combinations open to a central bank rather than how the exchange rate itself is determined.
rationales.C: The monetary approach essentially boils down to two assumptions: purchasing power parity holds, and inflation is determined by the money supply. Under these conditions PPP may describe exchange rate movements reasonably well over all but the shortest horizons, because money growth drives relative inflation and relative inflation drives the exchange rate.

questions.stem: The two main problems with estimating a constant variance-covariance (VCV) matrix from sample statistics are most likely that it:

options.A: cannot handle many assets, and has substantial sampling error.
options.B: requires normality, and cannot handle time variation.
options.C: requires a factor structure, and is biased in all cases.

rationales.A: Both problems apply. First, given typical sample periods, the method cannot be used to estimate the VCV matrix for large numbers of assets: if the number of assets exceeds the number of observations, the estimated matrix is singular and some portfolios will erroneously appear riskless. Second, given typical sample sizes, the method is subject to substantial sampling error. A useful rule of thumb is that the number of observations should be at least 10 times the number of assets.
rationales.B: Sample estimation of the VCV matrix does not rest on an assumption of normality, and a constant sample matrix handles time variation no worse than the alternatives it is being compared with. Neither item is one of the two problems identified.
rationales.C: Sample statistics require no factor structure at all, which is precisely what distinguishes the approach from a multi-factor VCV matrix, and sample covariances are unbiased on average. Their weakness is imprecision, not bias.

questions.stem: A rule of thumb for the number of observations needed for a reliable sample variance-covariance (VCV) matrix covering N assets is most likely:

options.A: 100 times N.
options.B: 10 times N.
options.C: 3 times N.

rationales.A: One hundred observations per asset is far above the guideline and would demand roughly a century of monthly data for even a modest asset list, a sample length over which the underlying covariances could hardly be treated as constant.
rationales.B: A useful rule of thumb is that the number of observations should be at least 10 times the number of assets for the sample VCV matrix to be deemed reliable. With materially fewer observations, sampling error in the estimated covariances is large, and once the number of observations falls below the number of assets the matrix is singular and some portfolios appear riskless.
rationales.C: Three observations per asset is well below the guideline. A matrix estimated that thinly would be dominated by sampling error, even though it has not yet become singular.
